ifgc-2021-ch4.title: 2021 International Fuel Gas Code, Chapter 4 Gas Piping Installations (Sections 401-402, Tables 402.4(2) and 402.4(3))
ifgc-2021-ch4.note: Read in the ICC Digital Codes free view. The site answers scripts with 403, so the automatic link check cannot confirm it. Only the rows the gas line page needs are quoted here, with table number and edition.
quotes: 401.4 Additional appliances. Where an additional appliance is to be served, the existing piping shall be checked to determine if it has adequate capacity for all appliances served. If inadequate, the existing system shall be enlarged as required or separate piping of adequate capacity shall be provided.

402.1 General considerations. Piping systems shall be of such size and so installed as to provide a supply of gas sufficient to meet the maximum demand and supply gas to each appliance inlet at not less than the minimum supply pressure required by the appliance.

402.2 Maximum gas demand. The volumetric flow rate of gas to be provided shall be the sum of the maximum input of the appliances served. The total connected hourly load shall be used as the basis for pipe sizing, assuming that all appliances could be operating at full capacity simultaneously. ... The volumetric flow rate of gas to be provided shall be adjusted for altitude where the installation is above 2,000 feet (610 m) in elevation.

402.3 Sizing. Gas piping shall be sized in accordance with one of the following: 1. Pipe sizing tables or sizing equations in accordance with Section 402.4 or 402.5 as applicable. 2. The sizing tables included in a listed piping system’s manufacturer’s installation instructions. 3. Engineering methods.

rheem-gas-piping.title: Gas Piping Information for Tankless Water Heaters (2018)
rheem-gas-piping.note: Rheem brochure hosted by a distributor (Kleen-Rite). Rheem says its information comes from NFPA 54 / ANSI Z223.1 (2012) and covers low-pressure natural gas in rigid iron pipe.
quotes: most tankless water heaters have a BTU capacity ranging from 140,000 to 200,000 or more, which makes a tankless water heater one of the largest single appliances on a typical gas system.

A typical residential gas system is a low-pressure system, meaning that the home is supplied with a gas pressure around 7 in. w.c. (inches of water column). The piping must be sized sufficiently enough so that the pressure drop is a half an inch of water column or less, when all the gas appliances are on.
In all cases, a near 200,000 BTU gas appliance will require a minimum of a ¾-inch gas supply line.

In the 2012 National Fuel Gas Code (NFPA54. ANSI Z223.1), a 3.0 in. w.c. pressure drop chart was added for certain conditions. This chart allows a 200,000 BTU gas appliance to be installed on a ½-inch gas line up to 40 ft. in length. However, the following conditions must be met: The minimum static gas pressure must be 8 in. w.c. or greater; The calculated dropped pressure (the static pressure minus the 3.0 in. pressure drop), must be greater than the highest minimum gas pressure required by any of the gas appliances on the system.
Each meter has a capacity in Cubic Feet per Hour (CFH). Locate that number regulator and multiply it by 1,024 (BTUH/CFH) to give you an approximate BTUH capacity for natural gas.

199,900 BTU Tankless, a 75,000 BTU Furnace, a 55,000 BTU Range, a 25,000 BTU Dryer, and a 40,000 BTU Gas Log Fireplace. The sum of these appliances is 394,900 BTU. ... Divide total BTU by 1,024 to get the estimated Cubic Feet per Hour (CFH) requirement for the meter and regulator; 386 CFH in our example.

If the water heater was a typical tank type at 40,000 BTU, then the overall system requirement would have been just 235,000 BTU with a meter and regulator rated at 235 Cubic Feet per Hour. A typical household meter and regulator is commonly rated at 250 Cubic Feet per Hour.
The local gas utility can provide more information on upgrading the meter and regulator for the home.

An undersized gas system can cause poor performance in the appliances. It could cause the burners to soot, pilots lights and burners to go out, or cause condensate to form in the heat exchanger of the furnace or water heater.

While a negative pressure gas valve in an appliance can operate at a very low gas pressure, it can have adverse effects on an undersized gas system. This style of appliance can actually rob the gas from other appliances, such as a furnace and possibly cause nuisance outages.
Each appliance is required to have a rating plate. This plate will list the BTU ratings of the appliance and required gas pressures for proper operation.

Items such as elbows, tees, and valves are not included in these sample calculations. Their equivalent pipe length should be included when sizing gas systems. It is recommend that a licensed gas tradesman size, design, and install the gas system.

aos-pilot-guide.title: How to relight a water heater’s pilot light
quotes: The information on this page should be considered secondary to the information in your water heater's instruction manual.
If the pilot light goes out, the thermocouple or thermopile will not be energized and the pilot safety valve will open. Gas will stop flowing to the pilot burner and the water heater shuts off.
But if the thermocouple itself is broken, the pilot safety valve in the gas valve will not receive power, and the pilot will not remain lit once the pilot knob is released.

The pilot light on a water heater is susceptible to changes in gas pressure. ... in some cases, gas pressure becomes an ongoing problem. This typically indicates an issue outside the water heater, perhaps with the external gas lines.
be on the lookout for drafts that could blow out the pilot light. Sometimes, an open door ... could be enough to allow a gust of wild to extinguish that small, somewhat fragile flame.

Without enough air, it may be impossible for your water heater to properly burn off fuel. This issue can result in unburned fuel and/or carbon monoxide being released into your home. It’s a dangerous situation. If you suspect a lack of air is causing issues with your pilot light, it’s vital you bring in a tech
Another possible reason your water heater’s pilot won’t light could be a kink or clog in the flex tubes linking your fuel supply and your gas controller.

the pilot control valve in your water heater can fail over time. If this is the reason behind an extinguished pilot light, you’ll need to call for a service visit, and the valve will most likely need to be replaced.
Most pilot lights can easily be relit at home by a homeowner or other resident
Do not continue if you smell gas.

review the lighting instructions for your water heater as located on the water heater’s label and/or in the owner’s manual that came with your unit. These instructions supersede the instructions in this guide.

aos-signature-manual.title: Signature 100 residential gas water heaters, direct vent: Installation Instructions and Use & Care Guide (100341469, March 2021)
quotes: Turn the gas control/temperature knob counterclockwise to the "OFF" setting. Wait ten (10) minutes to clear out any gas. If you then smell gas, STOP!

Press the gas control/temperature knob all the way in and hold it in. The knob should travel in about 1/4 inch if it is set to "PILOT" correctly. While holding the gas control/temperature knob in, click the igniter button continuously (about once a second) for up to 90 seconds or until Status Light begins to blink.

If the status light does not start blinking within 90 seconds, repeat steps 2 through 5 up to THREE (3) times, waiting 10 minutes between lighting attempts. The circuitry in this advanced gas valve requires that you wait 10 minutes between lighting attempts.
If the status light does not start blinking after three lighting attempts, turn the gas control/temperature knob to "OFF" and call a qualified service technician or your gas supplier.

PILOT WILL NOT LIGHT OR REMAIN LIT: 1. Air in gas line 2. No gas 3. Dirt in gas lines 4. Pilot line or orifice clogged 5. Defective thermopile 6. Insufficient combustion air 7. Gas control/thermostat ECO switch open 8. Defective igniter or electrode 9. Low gas pressure 10. Incorrect gas

0 FLASHES (LED NOT LIT): Pilot light is not lit or thermopile has not yet reached normal operating temperature. ... It may take up to 90 seconds of continuous Pilot operation before the thermopile reaches normal operating temperature and the Status Light starts to blink. ... If the Pilot is visible and the Status Light does not blink after 90 seconds of continuous Pilot operation, the Pilot flame may not be heating the thermopile sufficiently (weak Pilot), the thermopile may be defective, or wiring connectors may be loose.
RED LIGHT ON (SOLID): Pilot light was recently extinguished and the thermopile is cooling down. Turn Gas Control Valve/Thermostat knob to "OFF". Wait 10 minutes for the thermopile to cool
1 FLASH (EVERY 3 SECONDS): Normal operation. No corrective action necessary.

2 FLASHES: Pilot is lit but the thermopile is not producing the required output voltage. ... The thermopile is probably defective, but loose wiring connections or a weak Pilot flame can also cause this symptom.
4 FLASHES: The Gas Control Valve’s temperature sensor has detected that the water temperature was too high. ... Replace the Gas Control Valve/Thermostat.
5 FLASHES: The temperature sensor (thermistor) is defective.
7 FLASHES: Gas Control Valve failure. ... Replace the Gas Control Valve/Thermostat.
8 FLASHES: ... the pilot valve is stuck open. Turn the main gas supply "OFF". Replace the gas control valve/thermostat.

scald.source: A. O. Smith gas Use & Care Guide 100400765 (Table 1 and gas control settings); CPSC Publication 5098. A dash means the source gives no figure for that temperature.

tpCauses.caption: What a leaking relief valve is telling you

rows.see: A small drip from the discharge pipe, often after hot water use or overnight
rows.cause: Water pressure too high, or no working thermal expansion tank
rows.do: Check pressure with a gauge; a pressure-reducing valve set to 50–60 psi and a sized expansion tank are the usual fixes
rows.who: A. O. Smith gas manual

rows.see: A drip that started after you tested the valve
rows.cause: Debris or mineral scale holding the seat open
rows.do: Operate the lever once more to flush it; if it keeps dripping, have the valve inspected
rows.who: A. O. Smith gas manual

rows.see: A drip with pressure at 50–60 psi and a working expansion tank
rows.do: Have a qualified person replace the valve; do not repair it
rows.who: A. O. Smith gas manual; Watts tag

rows.see: A lot of very hot water or steam pouring out
rows.cause: The tank is overheating: a failed thermostat or gas control, or a shorted element on an electric tank
rows.do: Stand clear, turn the gas supply or the breaker off, and call a qualified person now
rows.who: A. O. Smith gas and electric manuals; Watts tag

rows.see: Nothing comes out when you lift the lever
rows.cause: The valve or its pipe is blocked by deposits
rows.do: Turn the water heater off and call a plumber; the tank has no working protection
rows.who: Watts tag; A. O. Smith gas manual

rows.see: A dripping expansion tank setup that still leaks
rows.cause: Expansion tank sized wrong, lost its air charge, or pressure still too high
rows.do: Check the tank's air charge matches house pressure (not above 80 psi) and its size
rows.who: A. O. Smith gas manual

tpCauses.source: A. O. Smith gas Use & Care Guide 100400765 (troubleshooting and T&P maintenance); A. O. Smith electric Use & Care Guide 2000598248; Watts relief valve warning tag

elementSymptoms.caption: Upper or lower element: what each failure looks like

rows.sign: Some hot water, but it runs out much sooner than it used to
rows.why: A. O. Smith: the lower element does most of the work and usually wears out first; the upper one still heats the top of the tank

rows.sign: No hot water at all, breaker on, reset button not tripped
rows.why: A. O. Smith lists a burned-out upper element among the causes of no hot water; its controls run only one element at a time

rows.sign: Reset button or breaker trips again soon after a reset
rows.why: A. O. Smith: a shorted element lets the tank overheat or draws too much current

rows.sign: Relief valve releases a lot of very hot water
rows.why: A. O. Smith electric manual; turn the breaker off first

rows.sign: Water seeping from the side of the tank at an access panel
rows.why: A. O. Smith: failed gaskets let water seep from the side of the tank where the elements pass through the steel

rows.sign: Error code naming the upper or lower element circuit (electronic models)
rows.why: A. O. Smith electronic models report which circuit failed

elementSymptoms.source: A. O. Smith electric Use & Care Guide 2000598248 (troubleshooting and diagnostic codes); A. O. Smith leaking guide

pilotStatus.caption: What the status light on a thermopile gas control means (A. O. Smith)

columns.label: What the manual says it means

rows.means: Pilot not lit, or lit but the thermopile has not warmed up yet; that can take up to 90 seconds of pilot flame
rows.who: Relight by the label; after three tries, a qualified technician or the gas supplier

rows.means: The pilot went out recently and the thermopile is cooling
rows.who: Knob to Off, wait 10 minutes, then relight by the label
Nothing to do

rows.means: Pilot is lit but the thermopile is not making enough voltage (weak pilot, loose wiring or a failed thermopile)
rows.who: Qualified technician

rows.means: The control saw water that was too hot and shut the pilot and burner off
rows.who: Gas control replacement: qualified technician
Qualified technician
Gas control replacement: qualified technician

rows.means: The thermopile is still making power with the knob off; the pilot valve may be stuck open
rows.who: Turn the main gas supply off; qualified technician

pilotStatus.source: A. O. Smith Signature 100 Use & Care Guide 100341469 (March 2021), status light and diagnostic code chart (meanings). The advice column is ours: where the manual's fix is a part replacement, we send it to a qualified technician. Other controls use other codes: read the chart in your own manual.

pilotCauses.caption: Why a pilot will not light or stay lit, and who fixes it

columns.label: Who the manual says fixes it

rows.sign: New heater or gas work just done; several tries before the pilot catches
rows.who: A. O. Smith: it may take several lighting attempts; Rheem: a qualified technician purges the line

rows.cause: No gas, low gas pressure or the wrong gas
rows.sign: Other gas appliances also act up; weak or small pilot flame
rows.who: Your gas utility or supplier (A. O. Smith)

rows.cause: Drafts or not enough combustion air
rows.sign: Pilot goes out at random, near an open door, vent or fan; yellow or lazy flame
rows.who: A technician, before relighting, if air supply is the problem (A. O. Smith); clear the area of clutter

rows.cause: Thermocouple or thermopile not making enough power
rows.sign: Pilot lights but goes out when you let go of the knob, or 2 flashes on the status light
rows.who: Qualified service technician (Rheem)

rows.cause: Clogged pilot orifice, pilot tube or dirt in the gas line
rows.sign: Pilot will not light, or the flame is small
rows.who: Qualified service technician (Rheem); utility for dirt in the line (A. O. Smith)

rows.cause: Energy cutoff (ECO) or thermal switch opened
rows.sign: Pilot and burner shut off after the water overheated; a code such as 4 flashes
rows.who: Gas control replacement by a qualified technician (Rheem)

rows.sign: Everything else checks out; 7 or 8 flashes
rows.who: Service visit; the valve usually has to be replaced (A. O. Smith)

rows.cause: Flammable vapor system (FVIR) has shut the heater down
rows.sign: After paint, gasoline or solvent use nearby, or a blocked air intake
rows.who: Do not relight; call a qualified person (A. O. Smith)

pilotCauses.source: A. O. Smith Signature 100 Use & Care Guide 100341469 troubleshooting chart, A. O. Smith residential gas Use & Care Guide 100400765, A. O. Smith pilot light guide, Rheem GG Series Use & Care Manual troubleshooting chart.
